sections.html:
Cambridge sits in Middlesex County directly across the Charles River from Boston. The 2020 census counted 118,403 residents on about 7 square miles, so a Cambridge house usually has close neighbors, and each parcel is valued and taxed on its own record. The city runs under a council-manager form of government, and the assessing and finance offices that handle your tax bill report to the city manager.

Demand follows the universities and the biotech and research employers around Kendall Square, and the squares, such as Harvard, Central, Inman and Porter, work as neighborhood centers. Heating systems, roofs and windows get heavy use through cold winters, so buyers' inspectors look at them closely.

Rent control ended in Massachusetts in 1994, and Cambridge's version had been unusually strict. Landlord-sellers with long-held rentals may still find old records worth checking.

sections.h2: Who bills Cambridge property tax and when
sections.html:
Assessing values the property and the Finance Department bills and collects. Cambridge bills twice a year. For FY2027 the first-half bill was issued October 19, 2026 and was due November 18, 2026, and the FY2027 rates are $6.95 per $1,000 residential and $16.99 per $1,000 commercial and industrial. Call the Finance Department for the second-half due date.

If your FY2027 first-half bill includes a water and sewer lien, contact the Finance Department at 617-349-4220. That office also handles municipal lien certificates and online payments.

sections.h2: How do I apply for the residential exemption?
sections.html:
The deadline is April 1 of the fiscal year, which for FY2027 means April 1, 2027. The exemption removes part of the value of an owner-occupied home from taxation, and Cambridge uses January 1 to test ownership and occupancy. For FY2027 the test date is January 1, 2026.

New owners should read this carefully. If you bought a Cambridge property and the exemption carried over from the previous owner, you must qualify on your own to keep it into the next fiscal year. Apply through the city's online portal, which requires a Viewpoint account, or ask Assessing for a paper form at 617-349-4343.

  • Other personal exemptions can be combined with it, but taxable value cannot fall below 10 percent of assessed value.
  • Income-related exemptions need a copy of the 2025 income tax return.
  • Assessing's office is at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, open Monday 8:30 to 8, Tuesday to Thursday 8:30 to 5, and Friday 8:30 to noon.

When you sell, the buyer is the one who needs to qualify. Do not tell a buyer the exemption will transfer.

sections.h2: Abatement: how it works and how urgent it is
sections.html:
The FY2027 abatement window runs from October 19 to November 18, 2026, the same date the first-half bill was due. Assessed values follow full and fair cash value, meaning 100 percent of fair market value, reached through cost, income and market approaches.

To dispute a value, file with Assessing by mail or in person and be ready to show recent comparable sales. Assessing held online help sessions during the abatement period, and staff can be reached at 617-349-4343 or assessors@cambridgema.gov. If the result is not what you want, the next level is the Appellate Tax Board, and the clock there is three months from the decision.

Ask Assessing how a pending request affects the bill you owe before you hold back any payment.

sections.h2: What closing a Cambridge sale involves
sections.html:
The state steps apply here as they do everywhere in Massachusetts. A real estate attorney is customary and expected, and the state's deeds excise is $2.28 for every $500 of the sales price. Deeds are recorded at the Registry of Deeds, and masslandrecords.com lets you search the state's land records yourself before you list.

A seller also needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale requirements, and the fire department charges a fee. Ask the Finance Department for a municipal lien certificate so you know exactly what is owed on the tax and any water or sewer lien before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: Income-based exemptions and records to pull
sections.html:
Beyond the residential exemption, Assessing handles personal exemptions that depend on age, income or other circumstances. Income-related ones need a copy of the 2025 income tax return, so owners who plan to apply should find that return before they call.

If you are selling, you will not be filing for the next fiscal year yourself, but the records still help. They show the buyer, the attorney and the lender what the house has been paying and why. Gather the last bill, the receipt for each payment and any letter Assessing sent after an abatement request.

Visit Assessing at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, if you prefer to ask in person, or write to assessors@cambridgema.gov. Staff can explain how a request in progress affects the bill you owe, which is worth knowing before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: Water and sewer charges on the tax bill
sections.html:
Cambridge runs its own municipal water system, and unpaid water and sewer charges can end up as a lien on the tax bill. That is why the lien certificate matters at a sale: it shows the tax and any water or sewer lien in one document.

If your first-half bill shows such a lien, call the Finance Department at 617-349-4220 before closing. Your attorney will want the figure, and a buyer's lender will want it paid or escrowed at the table.

sections.h2: Preparing to sell, step by step
sections.html:
A Cambridge sale goes faster when the tax side is settled early.

  1. Confirm the first-half bill, which was due November 18, 2026, was paid, and keep the receipt.
  2. Decide whether to file an abatement, since the window closes on that same date.
  3. Request a municipal lien certificate from the Finance Department.
  4. Order the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate from the local fire department.
  5. Tell your attorney whether you are receiving the residential exemption, so the buyer knows to apply on their own.

If the house needs work or has tenants, a cash buyer can close without the lender's repair list. The tax, lien and recording steps are the same for every buyer.

faqs.q: What is the Cambridge residential property tax rate for FY2027?
faqs.a: The FY2027 residential rate is $6.95 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the commercial and industrial rate is $16.99 per $1,000.

faqs.q: When is the first-half Cambridge tax bill due?
faqs.a: The first-half FY2027 real estate bill was issued October 19, 2026 and was due November 18, 2026. Cambridge bills twice a year, so call the Finance Department for the second-half date.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for a Cambridge abatement in FY2027?
faqs.a: The abatement period runs October 19 to November 18, 2026. Contact the Assessing Department at 617-349-4343 right away if you plan to file.

faqs.q: Will the residential exemption transfer to the buyer of my Cambridge house?
faqs.a: No, the buyer has to qualify on their own. A new owner who inherited the exemption must still qualify to keep receiving it in the next fiscal year.

faqs.q: How do I find out what is owed before selling a Cambridge house?
faqs.a: Request a municipal lien certificate from the Finance Department at 617-349-4220. That office also handles online payments.
